title: Germany's €800M Arms Surge to Israel Centers on Nuclear-Capable TKMS Submarine, Ukraine's Fire Point Scales Cruise Missile Output
subhead: Berlin approved more arms export licences to Israel in five months than the prior 20 combined, with the bulk tied to a TKMS-built submarine that could give Israel a sea-based second-strike option. Separately, Ukraine's Fire Point is now producing about 100 long-range cruise missiles a month, and Portugal signed a home-grown drone deal.

sections.heading: Germany's Arms Exports to Israel Surge, Anchored by a Submarine
sections.body:
Germany approved almost €800 million ($913 million) in arms export licences to Israel in the first five months of 2026 — more than in the previous 20 months combined, according to a Federal Foreign Office reply to a parliamentary question reported by Al Jazeera. Nearly all approvals were cleared in April and May. The government said more than 60 percent of the value is earmarked for a single, unnamed 'major maritime project', which analysts identify as a submarine built by TKMS.

The likely vessel is the INS Drakon, a nuclear-capable Dolphin II-class submarine estimated at €480 million ($548 million) that underwent its maiden voyage at Kiel and was handed over to the Israeli Navy last week, per German media. Reports suggest it could carry a vertical launching system (VLS) for nuclear-tipped cruise or ballistic missiles, which would make Israel only the second navy after South Korea to field VLS on an air-independent-propulsion conventionally powered submarine — and give it a sea-based second-strike capability. Germany is reportedly financing about 30 percent of the Drakon's cost and roughly a third of the future Dakar class.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a concrete shift in European arms policy toward Israel despite public opposition, and it quietly advances Israel's nuclear deterrence posture by adding a survivable sea leg. It also signals TKMS's rising export momentum — the firm was separately selected by Canada as preferred bidder for up to 12 submarines.

sections.heading: Ukraine's Fire Point Scales Cruise Missile and Drone Output
sections.body:
Ukraine's leading arms startup Fire Point is manufacturing about 100 long-range Flamingo cruise missiles a month, a rate its chief executive Iryna Terekh says can sustain an enduring deep-strike campaign hundreds of miles inside Russia, The Guardian reports. The firm also produces FP-1 and FP-2 fixed-wing drones at 'hundreds per day'. The Flamingo carries a 1,150 kg warhead, has a range of about 3,000 km, and costs just under $600,000 — far cheaper than a US Tomahawk at roughly $3.5 million.

Fire Point now operates from 83 factories inside Ukraine plus one in Denmark, employing about 6,000 people, up from 3,500 late last year. Terekh said missile and drone attacks using Fire Point munitions occur at a daily rate of 'on average five to 15', and that she is not aware of any recent deep-strike attack that did not involve its products. Lighter FP-1 drones, with a range beyond 1,000 miles, have been used against Russian oil refineries in a campaign that has cut their production by about 20 percent.
sections.whyItMatters: Fire Point's scale-up shows Ukraine's homegrown defense industry maturing into a genuine long-range strike capability independent of Western-supplied missiles — a structural change in the war's economics, where cheap Ukrainian munitions now reach targets that Western systems were long withheld from.

sections.heading: Portugal Buys Home-Grown Tekever AR5 Drones for Maritime Patrol
sections.body:
Portugal's Air Force has signed a contract with Portuguese firm Tekever to supply AR5 drones for maritime surveillance, with delivery due in early September, Euronews and European Pravda report. The AR5 has a wingspan of almost 8 metres, weighs about 200 kg, and is purpose-built for long-range maritime missions including exclusive economic zone monitoring. The deal, authorized by a November defence ministry order with a maximum budget of just over €7.79 million, also includes operator training, a ground control station and the ATLAS mission system.

Tekever, which also supplies AR5 systems to Ukraine for combat reconnaissance, said it will train Portuguese personnel in a first phase by September and a second phase from October to reach full operational readiness. The contract value was not disclosed.
sections.whyItMatters: The deal is a small but telling example of European states buying home-grown unmanned systems validated in Ukraine combat, and of the AR5's dual civilian-military utility — a pattern likely to grow as NATO members seek maritime domain awareness without relying on US platforms.

sections.heading: US Deploys Newest EW Aircraft to Fairford as Iran Campaign Weighs
sections.body:
Two EA-37B Compass Call electronic attack aircraft — the US Air Force's newest electronic warfare platform — deployed from Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, Arizona, to RAF Fairford in the UK, landing July 23, according to Air & Space Forces Magazine citing flight tracking and local spotters. The EA-37B, which replaces aging EC-130s, is designed for standoff jamming of enemy communications, radar and navigation. The Air Force now fields 5 of a planned 22 EA-37s; the type first saw real-world use in the Middle East in April during Operation Epic Fury.

Fairford also hosts around a dozen B-1B bombers stationed since spring; a B-1B struck Iran on July 21, the first US bomber use in the conflict since April. About 50,000 US troops are deployed in the Middle East, with 18 killed and over 480 wounded per Defense Department data posted July 22. F-16s and A-10s have also been spotted carrying Angry Kitten EW jamming pods in combat.
sections.whyItMatters: The EA-37B deployment underscores how electronic warfare has become central to the US air campaign against Iran, and how the UK is being used as a staging base for potential large-scale operations — a posture that carries its own escalation risk.

sections.heading: NATO Air Defense and Russian Power Centers Under Drone Pressure
sections.body: Two ongoing developments illustrate the reach of drone warfare. Romania, a NATO member, shot down a third Russian drone in three days over the Black Sea and summoned Russia's ambassador, with an F-16 intercepting the intruder, The Guardian and Al Jazeera reported in late July. Separately, Russia cancelled its St. Petersburg Navy Day parade for a second straight year amid the Ukrainian drone threat, with the cancellation coinciding with large-scale internet blackouts in the city, Kyiv Independent reported — a sign of Ukrainian drones' ability to threaten Russian power centers and disrupt state events.
sections.whyItMatters: These are incremental but telling: NATO's eastern flank is now routinely intercepting Russian drones over allied territory, while Russia's own symbolic naval display is being curtailed by the same unmanned-strike threat Ukraine is industrializing.

bottomLine: Today's defense picture is defined by two parallel industrial shifts. Germany's near-€800 million arms surge to Israel — anchored on a TKMS submarine that could give Israel a sea-based second-strike option — shows European export policy bending toward Israel despite public opposition, while TKMS rides a wave of naval export wins. In parallel, Ukraine's Fire Point is scaling cruise missile and drone output to roughly 100 long-range missiles a month, cementing a home-grown deep-strike capability that is reshaping the war's economics. Smaller moves — Portugal buying Tekever's Ukraine-proven AR5 drones, the US forward-deploying its newest EW aircraft to Fairford — round out a day of incremental but consequential defense industry movement.
sources: Al Jazeera, The Guardian, Euronews, European Pravda, Air & Space Forces Magazine, Kyiv Independent, Wikipedia (FP-5 Flamingo)
